query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the Al concentration in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys enhances phase stability by shifting the balance between configurational entropy and atomic size mismatch, thereby favoring the formation of a more stable phase mixture (e.g., an increased BCC fraction relative to FCC) that underpins high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A multiphase Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy produced via conventional casting and standard heat treatment, exhibiting a mixture of FCC and BCC phases at a baseline Al concentration.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the Al content (both increasing and decreasing relative to the baseline) while using a controlled heat-treatment schedule to ensure comparable processing conditions.
generation.conditions: Test samples under high-temperature conditions (to assess strength and environmental resistance), cryogenic conditions (to evaluate toughness), and radiation exposure (to gauge radiation tolerance), ensuring that all samples are processed identically except for Al concentration.
generation.structural_mediator: The relative phase fractions and stability of FCC and BCC phases, as measured by synchrotron X-ray diffraction.
generation.mechanism: Al content modulates the atomic size mismatch and configurational entropy within the alloy. Higher Al concentrations are predicted to favor a shift towards a more stable BCC phase (or a beneficial balanced mixture with FCC), which enhances the retention of mechanical strength at high temperatures and sustains performance under cryogenic and radiation conditions. This mechanism links the alloy’s microstructural phase equilibrium directly to its multifunctional performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy, samples with higher Al content should exhibit a measurable shift in phase balance (increased BCC phase fraction or a more optimal phase distribution) that correlates with improved high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness. Conversely, lower-than-baseline Al concentrations are expected to produce less stable phase fractions and diminished performance.
generation.baseline: The alloy with the standard, literature-based Al concentration showing a known multiphase (FCC/BCC) microstructure.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is limited to Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys processed via casting and conventional heat treatment without additional alloying elements or extreme processing conditions that introduce new phases or significant segregation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative influence of Al concentration on the phase fractions and the magnitude of resulting property changes remain uncertain, as interactions with the other elements and subtle processing variations may also affect performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy samples where the only variable is the Al concentration (e.g., a baseline composition, one with increased Al by ~10%, and one with decreased Al by ~10%), ensuring identical casting and heat treatment protocols. Conduct synchrotron X-ray diffraction to accurately quantify the FCC versus BCC phase fractions. Perform mechanical tests at high temperature, cryogenic temperature, and under controlled radiation exposure.
measurements: Phase fraction analysis (via synchrotron X-ray diffraction)
Radiation-induced property changes (e.g., swelling or embrittlement metrics)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the systematic variation in Al concentration does not produce the predicted shifts in phase fractions (i.e., no clear trend toward enhanced phase stability with higher Al) or if the mechanical and environmental properties do not correlate with the expected phase stability changes relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

High-entropy alloys offer a promising alternative in several high-technology applications concerning functional, safety and health aspects. Many of these new alloys compete with traditional structural materials in terms of mechanical characteristics. Understanding and controlling their properties are of the outmost importance in order to find the best single- or multiphase solutions for specific uses. Here, we employ first-principles alloy theory to address the micro-mechanical properties of five polymorphic high-entropy alloys in their face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) phases. Using the calculated elastic parameters, we analyze the mechanical stability, elastic anisotropy, and reveal a strong correlation between the polycrystalline moduli and the average valence electron concentration. We investigate the ideal shear strength of two selected alloys under shear loading and show that the hcp phase possesses more than two times larger intrinsic strength than that of the fcc phase. Recent developments of high-entropy alloys with high strength and high ductility draw attention to the metastability-engineering strategy. Using first-principle theory, here we demonstrate that reducing the Ta level in the refractory TiZrHfTax system destabilizes the body-centered cubic (bcc) phase and leads to the appearance of the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) phase embedded in the bcc matrix. The alloying-induced features of the elastic parameters for the cubic and hexagonal structures are mapped out in details, and strong sensitivity to the crystal lattice and chemistry is revealed. Results show softening of the bcc matrix with decreasing Ta concentration which ensures ductile behavior. However, the elastically nearly isotropic hcp precipitates possess enhanced resistance against shear which promotes strengthening of the TiZrHfTax dual-phase system. The present atomic-level insight provides strong evidence to the experimental observation, and emphasizes the significance of quantum-design for advanced multi-phase high-entropy alloys with excellent strength-ductility combinations.

The phase constituent and microhardness of the arc-melted 20Co-Cr-Fe-Ni alloys, in both as-cast state and after annealing at 1000 °C for 30 days, were experimentally investigated by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD). Experiment results indicated that a uniform, stable, single Face-Center Cubic (FCC) phase can be obtained in as-cast 20 Co-Cr-Fe-Ni alloys with less than 30 at.% Cr. Annealing at 1000 °C has no effect on their phase composition and microhardness. When the Cr content is above 40 at.%, the σ phase forms and its volume fraction increases with the Cr content, which leads to an increase in microhardness. Annealing at 1000 °C for 30 days can slightly decrease the volume fraction of the σ phase and slightly decrease the alloy microhardness. Except for the Fe-rich alloys, the alloy microhardness increases with the Cr content when the Co and Ni or the Co and Fe contents were fixed. Moreover, comparing with the thermodynamically calculated phase diagram based on the TCFE database, it has been proved that the calculation can predict the phase stability of the FCC phase and the 1000 °C isothermal section. frame.system: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys in a multiphase state (as synthesized via conventional casting or heat treatment) where phase stability directly impacts a range of performance properties.
frame.goal: To develop and test a single mechanistic hypothesis that explains the governing factors of phase stability in these alloys and correlates these factors with the retention of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
frame.limitation: The current lack of an integrated mechanistic explanation that simultaneously governs phase stability and accounts for the diverse performance requirements over a wide range of operating conditions.

frame.regime: Testing under varied regimes, including high-temperature conditions (to assess strength and environmental resistance), cryogenic temperatures (to evaluate toughness), and exposure to radiation environments (to gauge radiation tolerance).
prior_attempts: Previous studies have separately addressed phase stability using empirical phase diagrams or computational thermodynamics, and have linked individual properties (high-temperature strength, for instance) to specific microstructural features. However, these approaches have fallen short of providing a unified, testable mechanistic explanation that ties all these properties to overall phase stability.

decision.trend: Early work on high-entropy alloys, particularly those containing Al (e.g. in AlCoCrFeNi systems), first employed empirical synthesis and thermo‐mechanical processing (casting, rolling, annealing) to generate multiphase microstructures, noting that variation in composition and processing leads to inherited lamellar or decomposed structures that correlate with exceptional combinations of properties. More recent studies have used advanced synthesis (e.g. configurable targets) and in situ characterization to tune phase content and interfacial chemistry, suggesting that factors like atomic size mismatch, configurational entropy, and even magnetic interactions control phase transitions (e.g. FCC↔HCP) and thus influence mechanical and thermal properties. Despite these advances, a unified, mechanistic explanation linking phase stability to the retention of high‐temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness remains unresolved.
decision.unsolved: The open challenge is to develop and test a single, controlled mechanistic hypothesis that quantitatively links the phase stability of multiphase Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys with their diverse performance metrics. Specifically, there is a gap in explaining how compositional tuning (especially Al content) and processing-induced phenomena (e.g. residual stresses, microstructural evolution) dictate phase proportions and transitions, in turn governing the integrity of properties across widely different operating regimes. An observation that would falsify the hypothesis would be if, under controlled variation, the predicted shift in phase fractions (and corresponding property enhancements) did not occur or if a different mechanism dominated under specific temperature or radiation conditions.
decision.lever: Perform a systematic variation of the Al concentration in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys using a controlled heat-treatment schedule, with one baseline composition (e.g., a standard Al content known to yield a multiphase state) against which adjusted Al levels are compared. Key parameters would include measuring phase fractions via synchrotron X-ray diffraction and correlating them with mechanical tests (high-temperature strength, cryogenic toughness), environmental resistance, and radiation tolerance.
decision.why: This approach follows the trend of moving from empirical and observational studies to direct, controlled experiments aimed at isolating the influence of a single key variable – Al content – on phase stability. Given the identified gap in a unified mechanistic rationale, this controlled variable experiment will test the hypothesis that the interplay between configurational entropy and atomic size mismatch (modulated by Al concentration) governs the phase stability that underpins the alloy’s multifunctional performance. The predicted observations relative to the baseline, and the clear falsification criterion, satisfy the constraints and cues set by the research question.
